Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models \paperpdfauthorWeijian Luo, Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Tianyang Hu

Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models

Weijian Luo ††thanks: Equal contribution.††thanks: Project leader: pkulwj1994@icloud.com Affiliation: Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu    Yujian Chen11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Polyadic Research Group Affiliation: Peking University    Hao Jiang Affiliation: Polyadic Research Group Affiliation: SAGA Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen    Guang Cheng Affiliation: The University of California, Los Angeles    Tianyang Hu ††thanks: Corresponding author: hutianyang@cuhk.edu.cn Affiliation: Polyadic Research Group Affiliation: SAGA Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
Abstract

Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT ), combining feature and query–key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model’s underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.

1 Introduction

Autoregressive language models generate text by predicting tokens sequentially. Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative: they jointly refine continuous representations of a token sequence through iterative denoising or flow dynamics, allowing multiple token positions to be updated in parallel. Recent studies have explored a range of representations, training objectives, and generative dynamics, including one-hot flows, learned token embeddings, and latent-space models (Lee et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Meshchaninov et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). Despite their different formulations, these models share a central computational component: a neural backbone that maps noisy continuous states to predictions for language generation.

Much of the progress in CDLMs has focused on the formulation and learning of continuous generative processes, while the Transformer architectures that implement them have received comparatively less systematic attention. Existing models commonly inherit architectural choices from causal large language models (LLMs) or from Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) developed for image generation. These architectures provide useful starting points for methodological research, but their suitability for continuous language generation warrants closer examination. Causal LLMs are designed for next-token prediction, whereas image DiTs operate on continuous visual representations. CDLMs must recover discrete language tokens from noisy continuous states while coordinating noise-dependent computation, vocabulary prediction, and, when used, self-conditioning. These requirements motivate a central question:

  • •

    What Transformer architecture is best suited to continuous diffusion language models?

In this paper, we systematically study Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce LangDiT , a backbone designed for continuous language generation. Our central finding is that architectural choices effective in causal LLMs or image diffusion models do not necessarily yield the best performance in CDLMs. By varying the architecture within fixed model formulations, we show that architectural design can substantially improve generation performance. We first develop and evaluate LangDiT within LangFlow (Chen et al., 2026), then transfer it to Plaid-style CDLMs (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026). In each setting, we retain the underlying representation, objective formulation, and inference sampler to study architectural changes within each formulation. The Plaid adaptation reuses a subset of the design while retaining its native prediction interface.

We investigate three aspects of CDLM architecture. Within the backbone, we study how feature normalization and noise conditioning affect denoising. At the vocabulary interface, we examine how gradients through the likelihood shortcut affect the learning of token embeddings. For self-conditioning, we investigate how strongly previous predictions should guide subsequent denoising. A cumulative ablation study under shared training and evaluation settings measures the incremental effects of these components, leading to a reusable architecture that improves generation while preserving the underlying model formulation.

We evaluate LangDiT on OpenWebText unconditional generation at a sequence length of 1,024. A seven-stage LangFlow ladder tracks successive architectural changes (Figure 1). At 250k updates and 128 NFE under the same schedule, GenPPL decreases from 64.26 to 53.66, while mean per-sample unigram entropy changes from 5.416 to 5.391. Separately, a 660k LangFlow checkpoint and a 520k Plaid checkpoint from 1M-update plans reach GenPPL 21.72 and 11.33 at the larger sampling budget (Table 3). These extended-training scores accompany larger changes in entropy and do not isolate the effect of architecture from training budget. We distinguish these settings throughout the paper (Figure 2).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We conduct a systematic empirical study of six denoiser-design interventions in CDLMs, using a cumulative LangFlow ablation under shared training and evaluation settings.

  • •

    We introduce LangDiT , which combines backbone normalization and noise conditioning with likelihood-shortcut gradient routing, calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning.

  • •

    We demonstrate lower GenPPL in matched LangFlow comparisons and examine the reuse of compatible components in a Plaid-style formulation, reporting sampling cost and unigram entropy alongside generation perplexity.

Together, these findings establish architectural design as an important source of progress in CDLMs and provide a reusable foundation for further research on parallel language generation.

2 Related Work

Continuous language diffusion and flow.

Diffusion-LM and self-conditioned embedding diffusion established continuous denoising approaches to language generation (Li et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022), while CDCD and Plaid developed categorical diffusion and likelihood-based training (Dieleman et al., 2022; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023). Recent work explores flow maps (Lee et al., 2026), learned embeddings with information-based noise scheduling (Chen et al., 2026), architectural refinements (Yang et al., 2026), hyperspherical dynamics (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026), and embedding-space flow matching (Hu et al., 2026). We study architectural design within fixed LangFlow and Plaid-style formulations.

Latent representations and decoding.

CoDAR uses contextual autoregressive decoding (Shen et al., 2026), while LDLM jointly learns an encoder, denoiser, and decoder with controlled gradient interactions (Meshchaninov et al., 2026). Cola-DLM introduces a text VAE and latent prior (Guo et al., 2026), and AURORA-LM restricts the noisy-input pathway while preserving high-capacity latents (Liang et al., 2026). Analysis of ELF links token recovery to decoder margins and denoising trajectories (Du and Ma, 2026). Our changes operate within the existing codebook-based prediction interface.

Normalization and conditioning.

DiT and EDM2 emphasize adaptive conditioning and magnitude control in diffusion networks (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Karras et al., 2024). RMSNorm, nGPT, and query–key normalization provide complementary approaches to controlling representation and attention scales (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019; Loshchilov et al., 2025; Henry et al., 2020). Related work examines attention-entropy collapse (Zhai et al., 2023) and uses query–key RMSNorm in rectified-flow Transformers (Esser et al., 2024). We examine these normalization choices alongside noise-conditioning capacity in continuous language denoising.

Self-conditioning.

Analog Bits, self-conditioned embedding diffusion, and LangFlow use previous predictions to guide denoising (Chen et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2026). AURORA-LM addresses training–inference mismatch through trajectory consistency (Liang et al., 2026). Our entropy-based gate regulates bootstrap inputs during training while retaining the baseline loss formulation and inference sampler.

Discrete diffusion and evaluation.

MDLM, LLaDA, and iLLaDA advance masked diffusion language modeling (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026), while Duo connects uniform-state discrete diffusion to an underlying Gaussian process (Sahoo et al., 2025). Across diffusion families, likelihood rankings can differ from those based on generation quality and sampling cost (Sahoo et al., 2026); lower GenPPL can also accompany reduced distributional coverage (Franca and Tong, 2026). We therefore report GenPPL alongside mean per-sample unigram entropy, with explicit sampling budgets.

3 The Language Diffusion Transformer

LangDiT is a Transformer denoiser for continuous language generation. Its design addresses three components of denoising: processing noisy embeddings, predicting discrete tokens, and incorporating previous predictions through self-conditioning. We develop the architecture within a LangFlow-style baseline (Chen et al., 2026), retaining its continuous representation, training and noise-schedule objective formulations, and inference sampler across architectural variants. Table 1 summarizes the design choices.

3.1 Overall Denoising Pipeline

At each denoising step, an input projection combines noisy token embeddings zγz_{\gamma} with an optional self-conditioning estimate xSCx_{\mathrm{SC}}. A bidirectional Transformer processes the sequence through attention and feed-forward sublayers modulated by the noise level γ\gamma. An untied vocabulary head produces contextual logits, augmented by a gated likelihood shortcut that measures compatibility between the noisy state and the codebook. Softmax yields token probabilities, whose weighted embedding mean provides the clean-state estimate used for both sampler updates and subsequent self-conditioning. Figure 3(a) illustrates this pipeline with one Transformer block expanded.

Relative to the baseline, LangDiT introduces backbone RMSNorm for feature-scale control, query–key RMSNorm for attention-logit scale control, and wider noise conditioning for greater modulation capacity. The likelihood shortcut follows a Gaussian noise model (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). We detach its embedding matrix to block the direct codebook-gradient path, while a bounded gate controls its forward contribution. An entropy-based gate further regulates bootstrap self-conditioning during training (Figure 3(b)); inference retains the un-gated posterior-mean estimator for both self-conditioning and sampler updates.

We next summarize the LangFlow formulation underlying our architectural study.

3.2 Continuous Representation and Training Objective

LangFlow represents tokens with learned embeddings and generates language by transporting Gaussian noise toward these embeddings (Chen et al., 2026). Its denoiser predicts token probabilities, whose embedding mean supplies the continuous estimate required by the flow.

Clean embeddings and noisy inputs.

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the vocabulary, y1:L∈𝒱Ly_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} a token sequence, and E∈ℝ|𝒱|×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} a learned codebook. Each row is normalized to norm d\sqrt{d} and scaled by s=0.1s=0.1:

E~v=d​Ev∥Ev∥2,Cv=s​E~v,v∈𝒱.\widetilde{E}_{v}=\sqrt{d}\,\frac{E_{v}}{\lVert E_{v}\rVert_{2}},\qquad C_{v}=s\widetilde{E}_{v},\qquad v\in\mathcal{V}. (1)

The resulting clean-embedding table is C=s​E~C=s\widetilde{E}. A token sequence is represented by x0∈ℝL×dx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, with x0,i=Cyix_{0,i}=C_{y_{i}}.

For the log noise-to-signal ratio γ=log⁡(σγ2/αγ2)\gamma=\log(\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}/\alpha_{\gamma}^{2}), we define

αγ=sigmoid⁡(−γ),σγ=sigmoid⁡(γ),zγ=αγ​x0+σγ​ϵ,ϵi​j​∼i.i.d.​𝒩​(0,1).\begin{gathered}\alpha_{\gamma}=\sqrt{\operatorname{sigmoid}(-\gamma)},\qquad\sigma_{\gamma}=\sqrt{\operatorname{sigmoid}(\gamma)},\\ z_{\gamma}=\alpha_{\gamma}x_{0}+\sigma_{\gamma}\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1).\end{gathered} (2)

Noise is independent across positions and embedding dimensions. Larger γ\gamma corresponds to greater corruption: γ→+∞\gamma\to+\infty yields Gaussian noise, whereas γ→−∞\gamma\to-\infty recovers the clean state.

Token prediction objective.

The denoiser predicts pθ,i​(v∣zγ,γ,xSC)p_{\theta,i}(v\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma,x_{\mathrm{SC}}), the probability of token vv at position ii given the full noisy sequence. We use θ\theta collectively for the trainable denoiser parameters, including the codebook and, where applicable, the shortcut-gate parameters ψ\psi. The noise-schedule parameters are represented separately through π\pi. We suppress xSCx_{\mathrm{SC}} when it is not needed to distinguish the training and sampling procedures.

Training uses token-level cross-entropy:

ℒCE=𝔼y1:L∼pdata,γ∼π,ϵ[−1L∑i=1Llogpθ,i(yi∣zγ,γ)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}=\mathbb{E}_{y_{1:L}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\,\gamma\sim\pi,\,\epsilon}\left[-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\log p_{\theta,i}(y_{i}\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma)\right]. (3)

Here, pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is the training sequence distribution, and π\pi is the learned Gumbel distribution over noise levels used by LangFlow’s information-based scheduler (Chen et al., 2026). All variants retain this loss formulation and the baseline entropy-matching objective for the schedule.

For a fixed codebook and corruption process, the population optimum of cross-entropy recovers the token posterior when the model has sufficient capacity. The corresponding probability-weighted embedding mean therefore equals the conditional clean-state mean 𝔼[x0∣zγ,γ]\mathbb{E}[x_{0}\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma]. LangFlow formalizes this connection through Bregman-divergence flow matching (Chen et al., 2026), explaining how categorical prediction supports denoising and sampling in continuous space.

3.3 Noise-Conditioned Transformer Backbone

The backbone processes noisy embeddings while adapting to the noise level. We study normalization and noise conditioning as separate components: normalization controls feature scales, while conditioning supplies noise-dependent modulation.

Input and self-conditioning fusion.

The input state is

h0=zγ+P⁡([zγ;xSC]),h_{0}=z_{\gamma}+P([z_{\gamma};x_{\mathrm{SC}}]), (4)

where brackets denote concatenation along the feature dimension and P:ℝ2​d→ℝdP:\mathbb{R}^{2d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is a zero-initialized, bias-free linear projection applied independently at each position. The embedding and backbone widths are equal in this architecture. When self-conditioning is absent, xSC=0x_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.

Transformer blocks.

Each block contains bidirectional attention and a feed-forward sublayer, each with a noise-conditioned residual gate. Following DiT (Peebles and Xie, 2023), a noise embedding cγc_{\gamma} supplies the shifts, scales, and gates:

u\displaystyle u =h+ga​(cγ)⊙Attn⁡(moda⁡(Na​(h);cγ)),\displaystyle=h+g_{a}(c_{\gamma})\odot\operatorname{Attn}\!\left(\operatorname{mod}_{a}(N_{a}(h);c_{\gamma})\right),
h′\displaystyle h^{\prime} =u+gm​(cγ)⊙MLP⁡(modm⁡(Nm​(u);cγ)).\displaystyle=u+g_{m}(c_{\gamma})\odot\operatorname{MLP}\!\left(\operatorname{mod}_{m}(N_{m}(u);c_{\gamma})\right). (5)

The subscripts aa and mm identify the attention and MLP sublayers; block indices are omitted for readability. We write the affine modulation as

modj⁡(v;cγ)=(1+δj​(cγ))⊙v+βj​(cγ),j∈{a,m},\operatorname{mod}_{j}(v;c_{\gamma})=\bigl(1+\delta_{j}(c_{\gamma})\bigr)\odot v+\beta_{j}(c_{\gamma}),\qquad j\in\{a,m\}, (6)

where modulation vectors and residual gates are broadcast across sequence positions.

Backbone RMSNorm.

LayerNorm subtracts the feature mean before normalizing magnitude. To examine whether this re-centering is needed in embedding-space denoising, we replace the two pre-normalization layers in each Transformer block and the normalization layer in the vocabulary head with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019):

RMSNorm⁡(x)=g⊙xd−1​∑j=1dxj2+ε,ε=10−6.\RMSNorm(x)=g\odot\frac{x}{\sqrt{d^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{j}^{2}+\varepsilon}},\qquad\varepsilon=10^{-6}. (7)

The mean-square reduction is computed in FP32, and the output is cast to the projection dtype. Both normalization layers use a learned gain without a bias, so the replacement preserves the parameter count. RMSNorm rescales the input without removing its mean component. The ablation tests the effect of this change while retaining the baseline adaptive modulation.

Query–key RMSNorm.

Normalizing the input to attention does not directly constrain the magnitudes produced by the learned query and key projections. In dot-product attention, changes in ∥q∥​∥k∥\lVert q\rVert\lVert k\rVert alter logit scale independently of directional similarity. We therefore apply RMSNorm to each 64-dimensional query and key vector after the fused QKV projection and head reshape, before rotary position embeddings:

q^i,h=RMSNorm⁡(qi,h),k^i,h=RMSNorm⁡(ki,h).\widehat{q}_{i,h}=\RMSNorm(q_{i,h}),\qquad\widehat{k}_{i,h}=\RMSNorm(k_{i,h}). (8)

Queries and keys have separate learned gains, each shared across heads within a layer; values are unchanged. The design follows QK normalization (Henry et al., 2020) and its RMSNorm implementation in rectified-flow Transformers (Esser et al., 2024). For head dimension dhd_{h} and gain vectors gq,gkg_{q},g_{k}, the normalized dot-product logit obeys

|(Ri​q^)⊤​(Rj​k^)dh|≤dh​∥gq∥∞​∥gk∥∞,\left|\frac{(R_{i}\widehat{q})^{\top}(R_{j}\widehat{k})}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right|\leq\sqrt{d_{h}}\,\lVert g_{q}\rVert_{\infty}\lVert g_{k}\rVert_{\infty}, (9)

where Ri,RjR_{i},R_{j} are the orthogonal rotary-position transformations. The bound removes raw input norms from the right-hand side; it does not fix a temperature or bound learned gains over training. Appendix A.1 gives the derivation. The ablations assess whether this scale control improves generation.

Noise-conditioning capacity.

The conditioning vector supplies shifts, scales, and gates to all 12 Transformer blocks and modulation parameters to the vocabulary head. We increase its width from 128 to 256, changing the timestep MLP from →→128256\!\rightarrow\!128\!\rightarrow\!128 to →→256256\!\rightarrow\!256\!\rightarrow\!256. The input is a 256-dimensional sinusoidal encoding of γ\gamma, and the MLP uses SiLU after each linear layer. All adaptive-normalization projections and the shortcut gate receive the wider vector. This increases the capacity for noise-dependent modulation without changing the Transformer hidden width or feed-forward dimensions. The change adds 7.36M parameters, or 2.25% of the baseline; its ablation therefore includes a capacity increase and is not a parameter-matched test of conditioning alone.

Contextual vocabulary head.

After the Transformer blocks, an RMS-normalized, noise-modulated head maps hidden states to contextual vocabulary logits ℓraw,θ∈ℝL×|𝒱|\ell_{\mathrm{raw},\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times|\mathcal{V}|}. Its output weights are untied from the clean-embedding table CC. The head draws on the full noisy sequence, while the likelihood shortcut supplies direct evidence from each position.

3.4 Vocabulary Prediction with a Likelihood Shortcut

Under Gaussian corruption, the distance between a noisy state zγ,iz_{\gamma,i} and a token’s signal-scaled embedding αγ​Cv\alpha_{\gamma}C_{v} provides local evidence about that token. Because all codebook rows have the same norm, the Gaussian observation log-likelihood reduces to a scaled dot product, up to a token-independent constant.

The baseline adds this analytic likelihood shortcut to the contextual logits:

ℓθbase​(zγ,γ)=ℓraw,θ​(zγ,cγ)+cskip​(γ)​zγ​C⊤,cskip​(γ)=αγσγ2.\begin{gathered}\ell_{\theta}^{\mathrm{base}}(z_{\gamma},\gamma)=\ell_{\mathrm{raw},\theta}(z_{\gamma},c_{\gamma})+c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma)\,z_{\gamma}C^{\top},\\ c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma)=\frac{\alpha_{\gamma}}{\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}}.\end{gathered} (10)

This parameterization follows Plaid and LangFlow (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Chen et al., 2026). The equation shows the shortcut at full strength. During baseline training, its contribution is linearly warmed up over the first 5,000 optimization steps.

LangDiT modifies both the gradient path through this branch and its forward contribution:

ℓθours=ℓraw,θ+aψ​(γ)​cskip​(γ)​zγ​sg⁡[C]⊤.\ell_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ours}}=\ell_{\mathrm{raw},\theta}+a_{\psi}(\gamma)c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma)\,z_{\gamma}\operatorname{sg}[C]^{\top}. (11)

Here, sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient, and aψ​(γ)a_{\psi}(\gamma) is a learned bounded gate computed from cγc_{\gamma}. This gate calibrates the likelihood shortcut and is separate from the residual gates within the Transformer.

Stop-gradient leaves the forward logits unchanged at fixed parameters and removes only the gradient through the shortcut’s explicit codebook factor. The codebook remains trainable through noisy-state construction. Detachment therefore changes the optimization graph without changing the forward model class or adding parameters. Appendix A.3 derives the removed contribution; this identity does not itself establish gradient conflict.

Bounded calibration.

The contextual head sees the full noisy sequence and is not constrained to model a context-only prior. We therefore allow a structured adjustment of the shortcut’s contribution:

aψ​(γ)=exp⁡(clip⁡(fψ​(cγ),−log⁡2,log⁡2)).a_{\psi}(\gamma)=\exp\!\left(\operatorname{clip}(f_{\psi}(c_{\gamma}),-\log 2,\log 2)\right). (12)

Here fψf_{\psi} is a →→1256\!\rightarrow\!32\!\rightarrow\!1 MLP with SiLU activation and a zero-initialized final layer. Thus aψ∈[0.5,2]a_{\psi}\in[0.5,2] and initially equals one. Both baseline and modified models retain the 5,000-step linear shortcut warmup. Calibration changes the forward weighting, while detachment controls the direct codebook gradient. An unrestricted head could absorb a change in shortcut weighting, so this parameterization is not a correction to the Gaussian likelihood identity (Appendix A.2).

3.5 Self-Conditioning during Training and Sampling

Self-conditioning supplies a clean-state estimate as an auxiliary denoiser input. LangDiT changes how this input is weighted during training while preserving the estimate used by the inference sampler.

Training with gated self-conditioning.

Following the baseline, we use self-conditioning on 25% of training examples, adopting the bootstrap procedure used in prior work (Chen et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022). For these examples, the full denoiser is first evaluated at the current zγz_{\gamma} and γ\gamma, with self-conditioning set to zero. This bootstrap call runs without gradient tracking and produces a probability matrix pboot∈ℝL×|𝒱|p_{\mathrm{boot}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times|\mathcal{V}|}.

The bootstrap probabilities determine a clean-state estimate and its confidence weight:

μboot=pboot​C,xSCtrain=sg⁡[w⁡(pboot)⊙μboot],\mu_{\mathrm{boot}}=p_{\mathrm{boot}}C,\qquad x_{\mathrm{SC}}^{\mathrm{train}}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[w(p_{\mathrm{boot}})\odot\mu_{\mathrm{boot}}\right], (13)

where w⁡(pboot)∈ℝL×1w(p_{\mathrm{boot}})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 1} is broadcast across embedding dimensions. The weight at position ii is computed from the token entropy

Hi(pboot)=−∑v∈𝒱pboot,i(v)logpboot,i(v).H_{i}(p_{\mathrm{boot}})=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\mathrm{boot},i}(v)\log p_{\mathrm{boot},i}(v). (14)

The token-wise weight is

wi​(p)=clip⁡(1−Hi​(p)log⁡|𝒱|,0,1).w_{i}(p)=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(1-\frac{H_{i}(p)}{\log|\mathcal{V}|},0,1\right). (15)

It is zero for a uniform distribution and one for a one-hot distribution. The complete bootstrap input, including multiplication by the codebook, is computed without gradients. The main denoiser call receives the weighted estimate. The gate therefore controls the influence of the auxiliary input without changing the definition of μboot\mu_{\mathrm{boot}}. The bootstrap prediction is derived from the current training input; it does not come from an earlier sampling step. The remaining 75% of examples use zero self-conditioning.

Interpretation.

We use token entropy as a heuristic measure of bootstrap confidence. Our hypothesis is that attenuating diffuse bootstrap predictions during training reduces the denoiser’s reliance on unreliable auxiliary inputs. The gate changes the training feedback signal, while both the inference sampler and inference-time self-conditioning retain the unweighted posterior mean. Appendix A.4 distinguishes token entropy from uncertainty in embedding space and explains why confidence weighting should not be interpreted as an improved clean-state estimator.

Sampling with unweighted estimates.

Generation starts from Gaussian noise and proceeds from high to low γ\gamma using the baseline Euler–EDM sampler (Karras et al., 2022). The normalized corruption coordinates in Equation (2) correspond to the additive-noise coordinates

τγ=σγαγ=eγ/2,z¯γ=zγαγ=x0+τγ​ϵ,\tau_{\gamma}=\frac{\sigma_{\gamma}}{\alpha_{\gamma}}=e^{\gamma/2},\qquad\bar{z}_{\gamma}=\frac{z_{\gamma}}{\alpha_{\gamma}}=x_{0}+\tau_{\gamma}\epsilon, (16)

where τγ\tau_{\gamma} is the EDM noise scale. The denoiser receives the normalized state zγ=αγ​z¯γz_{\gamma}=\alpha_{\gamma}\bar{z}_{\gamma}.

At each non-final step, softmax applied to the combined logits yields token probabilities and the clean-state estimate

x^0,i=∑v∈𝒱pθ,i​(v∣zγ,γ,xSC)​Cv.\widehat{x}_{0,i}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta,i}(v\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma,x_{\mathrm{SC}})\,C_{v}. (17)

This unweighted estimate determines the solver update and supplies self-conditioning for the next denoising step. The first step uses zero self-conditioning. Sampling requires neither an additional bootstrap call nor entropy-based weighting, including for models trained with confidence-gated self-conditioning. The final prediction is decoded by token-wise argmax.

3.6 Adaptation to a Plaid-Style Formulation

Our Plaid-style baseline is our implementation of RePlaID (Yang et al., 2026): it combines a 16-dimensional spherical codebook, a likelihood-bound objective (NELBO), a learned noise schedule, and ancestral DDPM sampling with a 12-block, width-768 Transformer. It is not the original published Plaid checkpoint. Unlike LangFlow, its continuous-state width is 16 rather than 768, and its native projections map the noisy state and self-conditioning into the Transformer. Thus Equations (1) and (4) specify the LangFlow instantiation, not a replacement of Plaid’s representation or input interface.

The native shortcut already has selective codebook detachment on self-conditioned examples. The adapted model retains that rule rather than importing LangFlow’s unconditional branch detachment, and does not add the learned calibration gate. Both variants retain the 16-dimensional state, NELBO, learned schedule, and DDPM transitions. The reported adapted-model evaluations explicitly select unweighted inference self-conditioning; enabling its optional inference gate would be a separate sampling intervention. The extended run uses a 1M-update plan, with a resumed decay schedule and an evaluated 520k checkpoint; Appendix B.1 gives the optimization settings. This experiment assesses reuse of compatible components, not transfer of the entire LangFlow pipeline.

3.7 Implementation Details

For OpenWebText, LangDiT uses 12 Transformer blocks with embedding and hidden width d=768d=768, 12 attention heads of dimension 64, and feed-forward width 3072. For the LangFlow formulation, the input projection PP maps 1536 dimensions to 768 dimensions. Transformer depth and hidden width are retained from baseline.

Both the baseline and LangDiT use fused QKV projections, rotary position embeddings, GELU feed-forward layers, and zero-initialized adaptive-normalization projections. Configuration definitions and training settings are provided in Appendix C and B.

3.8 Architecture Variants

We evaluate the complete design through seven cumulative configurations: baseline LangFlow, followed by backbone RMSNorm, Q/K RMSNorm, increased conditioning width, shortcut detachment, learned calibration, and training-time confidence gating. Each row of Table 4 adds one modification to the preceding configuration, with a separate training run from scratch. The final row defines LangDiT , the architecture in Figure 3, with about 100M transformer parameters including the codebook and untied vocabulary projection. The cumulative ladder uses a 250k-update schedule; extended-training runs are reported separately.

4 Experiments

We distinguish a cumulative LangFlow ablation under shared training settings from evaluations of extended-training checkpoints and the Plaid-style adaptation. Checkpoint progress, planned training budget, sampling cost, and sample count are reported separately.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Data and optimization.

We train from scratch on OpenWebText using Qwen3 tokenization (151,936 output entries), document BOS/EOS markers, packing, a 10,000-document shuffle buffer, and random crops of 1,024 tokens. The LangFlow ablation uses a global batch of 512, AdamW with weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0, and a 250k-update schedule: 5k warmup steps to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} followed by cosine decay to 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}. All seven configurations share the data order, objective, schedule, and sampler. Training uses bfloat16, dropout 0.1, seed 42, and EMA decay 0.999. The separate extended-training schedules are described in Appendix B.1.

Generation and sampling cost.

All local results reported here use 1,024 unconditional samples of 1,024 model tokens, temperature 1, and EMA weights. Generation seeds are 0–1,023. LangFlow uses the Euler–EDM sampler with unweighted self-conditioning and final argmax decoding. Its NFE counts all denoiser calls. Plaid uses ancestral DDPM: KK reverse transitions require K+1K+1 model forwards, including the final denoiser call. We show this extra call explicitly. These conventions also apply to the qualitative examples in Appendix F.

Metrics.

We score decoded text with a frozen GPT-2 Large model. The evaluator uses GPT-2 tokenization, adds no special tokens, excludes padding, and truncates each sample to at most 1,024 evaluator tokens. Generator special tokens are removed in the clean-text field; the inline scorer falls back to raw decoded text if that field is empty. For tokenized sample xx of length TxT_{x}, corpus-level generation perplexity is

GenPPLr⁡(𝒮)=exp⁡(−∑x∈𝒮∑t=2Txlog⁡r⁡(xt∣x<t)∑x∈𝒮(Tx−1)+),\operatorname{GenPPL}_{r}(\mathcal{S})=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{t=2}^{T_{x}}\log r(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}(T_{x}-1)_{+}}\right), (18)

where (a)+=max⁡(a,0)(a)_{+}=\max(a,0); the first token has no preceding context and is not scored. Entropy denotes mean per-sample unigram entropy in nats, computed on the same truncated, non-padding GPT-2 token sequences, including their first tokens. Samples are weighted equally, not pooled into a corpus histogram (Appendix D). This lexical statistic does not establish semantic diversity or distributional coverage, so a lower GenPPL is not by itself evidence of better overall generation quality.

4.2 Generation Results

Comparison with public models.

Table 3 combines published autoregressive and diffusion results with our local LangFlow and Plaid-style results. Published OWT GenPPL includes 104.9 for MDLM, 103.6 for SEDD Uniform, 77.6 for Duo, 62.2 for FLM, 36.5 for LangFlow, and 35.9 for the autoregressive Transformer. The local rows identify actual checkpoint updates and denoiser calls, with checkpoints within 250k updates and extended-training results grouped separately.

Evaluation scope.

The public-model results retain their source’s training settings and evaluation protocols. In particular, the published LangFlow OWT evaluation uses GPT-2 tokenization, a 1M-update training schedule, 1,024 sampling steps, and sample-averaged perplexity. Our local evaluations use the corpus-level aggregation in Equation 18. The table therefore provides a broad comparison of reported results; architectural attribution uses the shared-schedule local comparison below.

Matched LangFlow comparison.

Under the shared 250k-update schedule, LangDiT reduces GenPPL from 64.26 to 53.66 at 128 NFE, a relative reduction of 16.5%. Mean per-sample unigram entropy changes from 5.416 to 5.391. The comparison holds the data order, batch size, objective formulation, and sampler fixed. The modified model has 334.45M parameters, compared with 327.09M for the baseline.

Additional checkpoints within 250k updates.

At 1,024 NFE, the paired LangFlow checkpoints at 180k updates yield GenPPL 41.98 and 24.04, with entropy 5.248 and 5.049. For RePlaID at 128 denoising steps, the available baseline and modified EMA evaluations are at 40k and 150k updates (52.32 and 38.14 GenPPL). At 1,024 steps they are at 220k and 250k updates (23.91 and 13.90). These RePlaID pairs differ in training progress, and the modified 250k checkpoint comes from a 1M-update plan. Figure 2(a) labels the actual checkpoints; these results describe performance within the update cap and do not isolate the effect of architecture under matched training.

Extended training and transfer.

The 660k LangFlow checkpoint reaches GenPPL 44.72 at 128 calls and 21.72 at 1,024 calls, with entropy decreasing from 5.391 to 5.056. The Plaid adaptation at 520k reaches 27.51 and 11.33 at 129 and 1,025 total calls, with entropy decreasing from 5.393 to 5.014. Thus the lower GenPPL at the larger sampling budget accompanies a larger entropy change. Both checkpoints belong to 1M-update plans; neither result is a completed 1M-step evaluation. These checkpoints characterize performance under extended training but do not isolate architectural effects. Section 3.6 specifies the components adapted to Plaid. The reported Plaid scores establish an application of the design under a different objective, but do not supply a matched baseline comparison for all six LangFlow interventions.

4.3 Cumulative Ablation and Analysis

Each row of Table 4 adds one change to the preceding configuration and is trained from scratch. Comparisons at 50k updates use identical sample counts, EMA conventions, and 128-NFE sampling. The table reports total parameters, including both the codebook and the untied vocabulary projection; these are distinct from the approximately 100M parameters in the Transformer and conditioning pathways.

Normalization and conditioning.

Backbone RMSNorm reduces 50k-step GenPPL from 87.48 to 84.41. Adding Q/K RMSNorm changes it only slightly, to 84.37, while widening noise conditioning reduces it further to 80.74. This early checkpoint alone understates the observed separation between the two normalization configurations: at 250k, R2 and R3 reach 60.76 and 57.86. The Q/K comparison therefore depends on training progress. The conditioning result includes a 7.36M-parameter capacity increase and cannot isolate the benefit of where that capacity is allocated.

Shortcut and training feedback.

On the current cumulative path, detachment reduces GenPPL from 80.74 to 79.35, and calibration reduces it to 74.03. Adding confidence-gated training self-conditioning produces the largest adjacent reduction, from 74.03 to 61.73. Overall, R1–R7 reduce GenPPL by 29.4% at 50k. These increments are conditional on earlier modifications; they are not independent contributions or evidence of statistical significance from a single training seed. Because inference uses unweighted self-conditioning throughout this ladder, the final increment reflects a change to training feedback rather than an inference gate. Constant-attenuation and interaction controls remain unreported (Appendix E).

Training progress and entropy.

Figure 1 shows the recorded trajectories, with intermediate configurations displayed only through 50k for clarity. At 180k, the baseline and full model have GenPPL 64.94 and 52.39, with entropy 5.410 and 5.385. The paired measurements support reading the GenPPL gains together with lexical-diversity changes. They do not establish the proposed optimization mechanisms: attention diagnostics and gradient-alignment measurements are not reported.

4.4 Parameters and Computational Cost

The full LangFlow model has 334.45M total parameters, compared with 327.09M for the baseline. Both counts include the 151,936×768151{,}936\times 768 codebook and the untied vocabulary-projection matrix. Excluding those two matrices leaves approximately 101.07M and 93.71M parameters, respectively, including conditioning and the remaining prediction-interface parameters. Q/K RMSNorm adds 1,536 parameters and calibration adds 8,257; the remaining increase comes from widening conditioning. Replacing backbone normalization, detaching the shortcut, and applying confidence gating add none.

Equal training updates and denoiser-call counts do not establish equal FLOPs or wall-clock time. No training-throughput or sampling-latency advantage is claimed. The fixed-ID generations in Appendix F cover all twelve evaluations in Figure 2, with multiple complete outputs per setting; they are not a matched quantitative comparison.

The results support improving CDLMs through changes to the denoiser backbone and its prediction and training interfaces. Within the cumulative LangFlow study, the largest adjacent GenPPL reduction at 50k updates comes from confidence-weighted training self-conditioning. The Plaid-style adaptation illustrates how compatible components can be reused while retaining a different continuous state space, objective, and sampler.

The study is limited to OWT-1024 at one backbone scale and one training seed. The cumulative ablation measures effects along a fixed design sequence, and wider conditioning increases parameter count. Parameter- and compute-matched comparisons, component-removal ablations, and additional seeds would help isolate individual effects and assess their robustness. Direct measurements of attention behavior and codebook gradients are also needed to test the proposed optimization explanations. The unmatched Plaid comparisons and extended-training results should be interpreted with their respective training budgets. Finally, GenPPL and unigram entropy capture limited aspects of generation quality; evaluation of coherence, semantic diversity, and distributional coverage remains necessary.

5 Conclusion

We have presented LangDiT , a Transformer backbone developed through a systematic study of architectural design for continuous diffusion language models. Its design separates feature-scale control from noise modulation, decouples the likelihood shortcut’s forward contribution from its direct codebook gradient, and distinguishes clean-state estimation from the weighting of self-conditioning inputs. Experiments on OWT-1024 demonstrate improved generation performance within LangFlow and an adaptation of compatible components to a Plaid-style model, while preserving each model’s representation, objective formulation, and inference sampler. Evaluating GenPPL alongside unigram entropy allows these gains to be interpreted together with changes in lexical diversity. These findings highlight architecture as a reusable source of improvement in CDLMs and motivate further study at larger scales and across broader generation tasks.

Appendix A Architectural Analysis and Derivations

This appendix derives the normalization, likelihood, gradient, and estimation identities used to motivate LangDiT . The analysis characterizes the architectural interventions without establishing convergence or generation-quality guarantees. We assume real arithmetic, nonzero codebook rows, and finite noise levels with σγ>0\sigma_{\gamma}>0.

We retain the codebook notation C=s​E~∈ℝ|𝒱|×dC=s\widetilde{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} from Equation (1), so each row has squared norm s2​ds^{2}d. Single-position embeddings are treated as column vectors: cv=Cv,:⊤c_{v}=C_{v,:}^{\top} denotes the embedding of token vv, and zγ,i∈ℝdz_{\gamma,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the column-vector representation of the noisy embedding at position ii. The full noisy sequence remains zγ∈ℝL×dz_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}.

A.1 Scale Dependence of Normalized Attention

For a query vector q∈ℝdhq\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} and learned gain gq∈ℝdhg_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, define

q^=gq⊙q∥q∥22/dh+ε,ε>0.\widehat{q}=\frac{g_{q}\odot q}{\sqrt{\lVert q\rVert_{2}^{2}/d_{h}+\varepsilon}},\qquad\varepsilon>0.

Then

∥q^∥22≤∥gq∥∞2​∥q∥22∥q∥22/dh+ε≤dh​∥gq∥∞2.\lVert\widehat{q}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\lVert g_{q}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\frac{\lVert q\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\lVert q\rVert_{2}^{2}/d_{h}+\varepsilon}\leq d_{h}\lVert g_{q}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}. (19)

The same argument applies to a normalized key k^\widehat{k} with gain gkg_{k}. Let RiR_{i} and RjR_{j} denote the orthogonal rotary transformations at query position ii and key position jj. For standard scaled dot-product attention, norm preservation and Cauchy–Schwarz give

|⟨Ri​q^i,Rj​k^j⟩dh|≤dh​∥gq∥∞​∥gk∥∞.\left|\frac{\langle R_{i}\widehat{q}_{i},R_{j}\widehat{k}_{j}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right|\leq\sqrt{d_{h}}\,\lVert g_{q}\rVert_{\infty}\lVert g_{k}\rVert_{\infty}. (20)

This bounds the dot-product contribution to the attention logits before softmax; any separate additive attention bias must be considered independently.

For fixed gains, the bound is independent of the raw query and key norms. Exact invariance to positive rescaling holds for nonzero inputs when ε=0\varepsilon=0. With ε>0\varepsilon>0, it holds approximately when ε\varepsilon is negligible relative to the mean squared magnitude of both the original and rescaled inputs. Learned gains can nevertheless grow, and attention may remain concentrated. These bounds motivate examining feature scales and attention entropy, rather than establishing that query–key RMSNorm prevents instability or entropy collapse (Henry et al., 2020; Zhai et al., 2023).

A.2 Observation Evidence and Contextual Prediction

Hold the codebook fixed, and let p⋆p_{\star} denote the joint distribution induced by the data and the forward corruption process. For token vv at position ii, Equation (2) gives

log⁡p⋆​(zγ,i∣yi=v,γ)\displaystyle\log p_{\star}(z_{\gamma,i}\mid y_{i}=v,\gamma) =−∥zγ,i−αγ​cv∥222​σγ2+κγ\displaystyle=-\frac{\lVert z_{\gamma,i}-\alpha_{\gamma}c_{v}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}}+\kappa_{\gamma}
=αγσγ2​zγ,i⊤​cv−αγ22​σγ2​∥cv∥22+κ⁡(zγ,i,γ),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{\gamma}}{\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}}z_{\gamma,i}^{\top}c_{v}-\frac{\alpha_{\gamma}^{2}}{2\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}}\lVert c_{v}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\kappa(z_{\gamma,i},\gamma), (21)

where κγ\kappa_{\gamma} and κ⁡(zγ,i,γ)\kappa(z_{\gamma,i},\gamma) are independent of token identity. Since ∥cv∥22=s2​d\lVert c_{v}\rVert_{2}^{2}=s^{2}d, the norm-dependent term is also constant across tokens. The remaining token-dependent term is the baseline likelihood shortcut used in Plaid and LangFlow (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Chen et al., 2026).

Let zγ,−iz_{\gamma,-i} denote the noisy sequence with position ii removed. Under independent position-wise Gaussian corruption, zγ,iz_{\gamma,i} is conditionally independent of zγ,−iz_{\gamma,-i} given yiy_{i} and γ\gamma. For tokens vv and uu with positive conditional probability given zγ,−iz_{\gamma,-i} and γ\gamma, Bayes’ rule yields

log⁡p⋆​(yi=v∣zγ,γ)p⋆​(yi=u∣zγ,γ)\displaystyle\log\frac{p_{\star}(y_{i}=v\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma)}{p_{\star}(y_{i}=u\mid z_{\gamma},\gamma)} =αγσγ2​zγ,i⊤​(cv−cu)\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{\gamma}}{\sigma_{\gamma}^{2}}z_{\gamma,i}^{\top}(c_{v}-c_{u})
+log⁡p⋆​(yi=v∣zγ,−i,γ)p⋆​(yi=u∣zγ,−i,γ).\displaystyle\quad+\log\frac{p_{\star}(y_{i}=v\mid z_{\gamma,-i},\gamma)}{p_{\star}(y_{i}=u\mid z_{\gamma,-i},\gamma)}. (22)

The first term is local observation evidence. The second incorporates the other noisy positions and the token prior, so no uniform-prior assumption is required. With unequal embedding norms, the corresponding difference of norm-dependent terms from Equation (21) must also be retained.

The learned vocabulary head receives the entire noisy sequence, including position ii, and therefore need not represent a context-only prior. At fixed CC, an unrestricted head also admits an equivalent forward representation with an ungated shortcut:

ℓraw′=ℓraw+(aψ​(γ)−1)​cskip​(γ)​zγ​C⊤.\ell_{\mathrm{raw}}^{\prime}=\ell_{\mathrm{raw}}+(a_{\psi}(\gamma)-1)c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma)z_{\gamma}C^{\top}. (23)

Adding cskip​(γ)​zγ​C⊤c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma)z_{\gamma}C^{\top} to ℓraw′\ell_{\mathrm{raw}}^{\prime} recovers the gated logits. Thus, the decomposition into contextual logits and shortcut evidence is not uniquely identifiable from the combined logits alone. This forward equivalence does not imply equivalent gradients or optimization dynamics. In a finite architecture, the explicit gate may also affect approximation capacity.

A.3 The Gradient Path Removed by Detachment

Consider a single position after shortcut warmup. Write z=zγ,iz=z_{\gamma,i} and let β=aψ​(γ)​cskip​(γ)\beta=a_{\psi}(\gamma)c_{\mathrm{skip}}(\gamma) be a scalar. The logits, represented as a column vector, are

ℓ=r+β​C​z,r∈ℝ|𝒱|.\ell=r+\beta Cz,\qquad r\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}.

For the unweighted token cross-entropy loss ℒtok=−log⁡pθ​(y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=-\log p_{\theta}(y), where pθ=softmax⁡(ℓ)p_{\theta}=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell),

δ=∂ℒtok∂ℓ=pθ−onehot⁡(y).\delta=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}}{\partial\ell}=p_{\theta}-\operatorname{onehot}(y).

The direct gradient contribution through the explicit CC factor is therefore β​δ​z⊤\beta\delta z^{\top}.

Let gEg_{E} and gEsgg_{E}^{\mathrm{sg}} denote the gradients with respect to vec⁡(E)\operatorname{vec}(E) returned by backpropagation through the original and detached computational graphs, respectively. Define

JC=∂vec⁡(C)∂vec⁡(E).J_{C}=\frac{\partial\operatorname{vec}(C)}{\partial\operatorname{vec}(E)}.

Then

gE−gEsg=JC⊤​vec⁡(β​δ​z⊤).g_{E}-g_{E}^{\mathrm{sg}}=J_{C}^{\top}\operatorname{vec}\!\left(\beta\delta z^{\top}\right). (24)

Both gradients are evaluated at the same parameter values, with identical forward computations; the only difference is stop-gradient on the shortcut’s explicit CC factor. Paths through rr, through zz when the noisy state depends on the codebook, and through any other retained computation remain in both graphs. Batch and sequence averaging introduce their usual scaling factors, and the warmup coefficient can be absorbed into β\beta. Fixed token weights multiply the corresponding gradient contributions.

Equation (24) follows by differentiating the matrix product and applying the chain rule through codebook normalization. It identifies the removed contribution without determining whether that contribution helps or hinders optimization. In particular, a large cskipc_{\mathrm{skip}} does not by itself imply a large gradient, because δ\delta depends on the prediction. Relative gradient norms and alignment with the retained gradient provide more direct evidence for an optimization-based explanation.

A.4 Posterior Means, Geometry, and Self-Conditioning

For any distribution pp over tokens, let Y∼pY\sim p, X=cYX=c_{Y}, μ​(p)=𝔼p​[X]\mu(p)=\mathbb{E}_{p}[X], and

ℛp​(a)=𝔼p​∥X−a∥22.\mathcal{R}_{p}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\lVert X-a\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Expanding the square and using 𝔼p​[X−μ⁡(p)]=0\mathbb{E}_{p}[X-\mu(p)]=0 gives

ℛp​(a)=ℛp​(μ⁡(p))+∥a−μ⁡(p)∥22.\mathcal{R}_{p}(a)=\mathcal{R}_{p}(\mu(p))+\lVert a-\mu(p)\rVert_{2}^{2}. (25)

For a scalar weight w=w⁡(p)w=w(p), substituting a=w​μ​(p)a=w\mu(p) yields

ℛp​(w​μ​(p))−ℛp​(μ⁡(p))=(1−w)2​∥μ⁡(p)∥22≥0.\mathcal{R}_{p}(w\mu(p))-\mathcal{R}_{p}(\mu(p))=(1-w)^{2}\lVert\mu(p)\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 0. (26)

The equal-norm codebook further implies

tr⁡Covp⁡(X)=ℛp​(μ⁡(p))=s2​d−∥μ⁡(p)∥22.\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}_{p}(X)=\mathcal{R}_{p}(\mu(p))=s^{2}d-\lVert\mu(p)\rVert_{2}^{2}. (27)

These identities hold under any pp, whether or not it is calibrated. They describe conditional data risk when pp equals the true token posterior.

Entropy alone does not determine the embedding variance. For d≥2d\geq 2, let b1,b2b_{1},b_{2} be orthogonal unit basis vectors and set R=s​dR=s\sqrt{d}. Consider equal-norm embeddings c1=R​b1c_{1}=Rb_{1}, c2=R​b2c_{2}=Rb_{2}, and c3=−R​b1c_{3}=-Rb_{1}. Two distributions supported on these tokens, with probabilities (1/2,1/2,0)(1/2,1/2,0) and (1/2,0,1/2)(1/2,0,1/2), both have entropy log⁡2\log 2, but their embedding variances are R2/2R^{2}/2 and R2R^{2}, respectively. Entropy-based gating therefore provides a heuristic for auxiliary-input weighting, rather than an exact measure of uncertainty in embedding space.

In LangDiT , confidence weighting changes only the training bootstrap input. Both the inference solver and its self-conditioning input retain the unweighted mean. The risk identities above concern a single estimate under a fixed distribution; their implications for iterative generation must be assessed separately. This distinction motivates evaluating auxiliary conditioning and state estimation as separate aspects of the model.

Appendix B Implementation Configuration

Table 5 summarizes the shared training configuration and evaluation protocols for the cumulative architectural ablation. The 250k-update budget is the configured training target; each reported measurement is associated with its recorded checkpoint step. The shared-schedule ablation and the separate extended-training checkpoints are reported separately.

The denoising pipeline is described in Section 3.1, with its components detailed in Sections 3.3–3.5. For variants using RMSNorm, all normalization reductions are performed in FP32 with ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6}. In R3–R7, query–key RMSNorm is applied after projection and head reshaping, before RoPE. Each layer has separate query and key gain vectors of dimension 64, shared across attention heads.

Entropy-based confidence weighting is introduced only in R7. It acts on the bootstrap input for self-conditioned training examples. During inference, both self-conditioning and the solver update use the unweighted estimated posterior mean.

B.1 Separate Extended-Training Runs

The extended LangFlow + LangDiT result is evaluated at 660k updates after continued training of the full architecture under a separate 1M-update plan. The configured decay is indexed from step 270k, with 2,500 warmup updates, peak learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, and cosine decay toward 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} at step 1M. Training resumes from the 450k checkpoint, while retaining the decay schedule indexed from 270k. Global batch size is 512, weight decay is 0.01, and EMA decay is 0.999. These settings are separate from the 250k ablation schedule.

The extended Plaid + LangDiT result is evaluated at 520k updates. Its initial training stage uses a 1M-update target with 2,500 warmup updates followed by constant group learning rates: 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} for the backbone/projections and 10−210^{-2} for the embedding and schedule groups. The continuation resumes at 250k, uses 5,000 warmup updates, and then applies cosine decay to 0.1 times each group’s peak rate by step 1M. AdamW uses betas (0.9,0.999)(0.9,0.999), zero weight decay except 0.1 on the noise-schedule bounds, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Both stages use batch size 512, bfloat16, seed 42, and EMA decay 0.999. The OWT pipeline and tokenizer match those described in Section 4.1.

All extended-training results in Table 3 use plain, unweighted inference self-conditioning. The release metadata records the source run, actual checkpoint step, planned target, and sampling mode separately. The selected results do not imply that the 1M-update targets have been reached.

Appendix C Ablation Configurations

Table 6 summarizes the seven cumulative configurations used in Table 4 and the training trajectories in Figure 1.

R7 is the full LangDiT configuration illustrated in Figure 3, with an explicit 250k-update training budget. The 1M-update configuration is treated as a separate experiment. In the cumulative ladder, R4 widens noise conditioning to 256 dimensions, and R5 adds shortcut detachment at that width.

The 50k-step column of Table 4 uses the GenPPL scalar recorded at optimizer step 50,000 for each configuration. These values are neither minima nor averages over earlier checkpoints. The 250k comparison in Table 3 uses R1 and R7 under the same 250k schedule.

Appendix D Evaluation and Reporting Details

Matched ablations compare the same checkpoint steps, EMA conventions, generation seeds, sampling temperatures, NFE, and sample counts. The prescribed generation length is 1,024 tokens. Both the logged trajectories and the additional checkpoint evaluations reported here use 1,024 samples.

Metric definitions.

GenPPL is the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood aggregated over scored tokens, as defined in Equation (18). Unigram entropy is averaged across individual samples. For MM evaluated samples with empirical token-frequency distributions q^m\widehat{q}_{m}, this is

Hsample=1M∑m=1M[−∑vq^m(v)logq^m(v)].H_{\mathrm{sample}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left[-\sum_{v}\widehat{q}_{m}(v)\log\widehat{q}_{m}(v)\right]. (28)

Each q^m\widehat{q}_{m} is normalized within its sample; samples are not pooled into a single token-frequency distribution. We refer to this metric as mean per-sample unigram entropy.

Sample accounting.

The reported checkpoint metrics correspond to files containing 1,024 generated records. Texts shorter than two evaluator tokens contribute no next-token predictions to GenPPL; entropy is computed on their non-padding token sequences. The inline scorer’s empty-clean-text fallback is described in Section 4.1.

Logged-scalar extraction.

The training curves in Figure 1 and the 50k-step results in Table 4 are extracted from the training logs for R1–R7. The recorded hyperparameters specify EMA weights, 1,024 samples of length 1,024, 128 NFE, temperature 1, generation seed 0, and the same frozen GPT-2 Large scorer. The generation seed is distinct from the training seed of 42. The tokenizer and special-token policy are specified in Section 4.1; unigram entropy uses natural logarithms.

The exporter preserves exact optimizer-step indices and raw scalar precision in CSV files, records source-event paths and snapshot checksums, and rounds only the displayed values. Missing TensorBoard measurements are not imputed from other evaluations. These logs are reported with their actual checkpoint steps and evaluation settings.

Sampler provenance.

R7 applies confidence weighting to the training bootstrap input while retaining the baseline unweighted self-conditioning rule during sampling. A model implementation that also weights inference-time feedback defines a different sampling setting and falls outside the designated R7 comparison. Model class, code revision, sampler implementation, and feedback rule are therefore needed to identify an evaluation unambiguously.

Appendix E Limitations and Further Controls

The cumulative ladder measures successive changes in a particular order. It does not by itself establish the contribution of each component in the full architecture or resolve interactions among components. Further controls would include removing individual components from the full model, crossing query–key normalization with conditioning width 128/256, and crossing shortcut detachment with calibration at a fixed conditioning width. A backbone expansion with a comparable parameter increase, together with a separate compute-matched comparison, would further clarify whether gains arise from the placement of conditioning capacity.

The roles of the two gates also warrant separate tests. Comparing a fixed unit multiplier, a learned constant, and a learned noise-dependent multiplier would isolate the value of noise-dependent shortcut calibration. Comparing confidence gating with no gating, constant attenuation, and gates shuffled within noise bins would distinguish token-specific confidence information from generic attenuation. These controls are not included among the reported results.

Such comparisons would require matched data exposure and optimization schedules, comparable tuning budgets, and explicit accounting of parameter counts and FLOPs. Independent baseline and modified-model runs across a shared seed set would assess training variability; intervals obtained by resampling generated texts do not capture that source of uncertainty.

Potential failure modes include suppressing useful uncertain self-conditioning inputs or removing shortcut gradients that aid optimization. Lower feature variance alone does not establish better generation. These possibilities limit the generality of conclusions drawn from the present configurations and motivate evaluating the interventions across broader settings.

Appendix F Qualitative Generations

We present some unconditional generations covering every checkpoint and sampling budget shown in Figure 2. Panel (a) contributes eight baseline/modified evaluations from LangFlow and RePlaID within 250k updates; the RePlaID pairs differ in checkpoint progress, and its modified 250k checkpoint belongs to a 1M-update plan. Panel (b) contributes four extended-training evaluations from LangFlow at 660k and RePlaID at 520k, both from 1M-update plans. Table 3 reports the corresponding checkpoints and evaluation results.

Example selection.

From each of the twelve evaluation files, we display the fixed sample IDs. The evaluation settings follow the twelve bars in Figure 2; individual samples are not ranked by perplexity, fluency, or perceived quality. The GenPPL shown on each card describes its full 1,024-sample evaluation, not the displayed text alone; the paired entropy is reported in Table 3. The examples follow the figure’s panel and bar order.

Sampling settings.

All examples use EMA weights, length 1,024 model tokens, temperature 1, final argmax decoding, and unweighted inference self-conditioning. LangFlow uses Euler–EDM with 128 or 1,024 total denoiser calls. RePlaID uses ancestral DDPM with 128 or 1,024 reverse transitions plus one final call, for totals of 129 or 1,025; the card headers denote this extra call by “(+1).” The generation seed equals the sample ID. Equal recorded seeds do not imply semantic prompts or establish identical initial noise across formulations.

Reading the examples.

The complete decoded text is reproduced without correction or truncation, including special tokens and document boundaries. Names, quotations, citation-like strings, repetitions, and factual errors are part of the generated output. The nonprinting code points U+0097/U+009D, the source replacement character U+FFFD, and an unsupported ribbon emoji are displayed by code point (e.g., [U+1F380]). U+200B retains zero-width spacing and U+200E retains left-to-right directionality. Other changes are limited to typographic escaping and layout. These fixed-ID examples illustrate the cited evaluations but do not establish typical quality, factual accuracy, or systematic improvement with NFE.

White had worked as a band assistant at the Federal-Madland School from 2010 to 2017. White previously led the club’s dance room as chief of staff, according to sources close to the school’s leader, Federal-Madland President PJ York.

No criminal charges have been brought against the school, the Walldale School District, the Smyrna School District or the high school band’s president of the district, Ray Beckman.

Several members of the club have been responding to death threats, including 13-year-old teen Billy Goldman, who appeared on stage on Thursday and demanded that a man killed at the club not be identified by the police.

District Attorney Green and Mayor Charlie Pines, however, described the release as "ridiculous" and urged further investigation.

The shooting occurred in an upscale field near the club and its main host. The clubs are divided into groups of public school, business-school, black and special needs groups.

Florida Police Chief Kevin Evans said his department has been working overtime to assist with the investigation.

History [ edit ]

Route [ edit ]

The Mississauga bridge rises at the base of the Cumberland Estuary. It passes through Peterborough, Wallace Bay and Port Rupert to the west, part of Montreal to the north. From the time the bridge crosses the river, the roadway is seperated from the future. The bridge crosses Toronto and Mississauga and is a section of the Surrey Freeway Line. In 1967, the Montreal River Reservoir line began funneling into the southeast of Mississauga. Water was taken from this route south of Peterborough after a power attraction broke.[10]

The bridge was proposed in 1970 with the support of the Ally Vance Corporation. In 1972, the company decided to forge a bridge based solely on air and hydroelectric to the Huroe Valley.[5] In 1974, the bridge was completed and financed by the federal government. The BIS was tasked with planning an ambitious bridge plan, and the corporation established its Budget and Development Board to help the railway secure contracts. The BIS engaged primarily in grants and expenses associated with economic projects (including funding). As a result the bridges were flooded, with sections of the bridge being sent over to be diverted into the river.

Work [ edit ]

The original bridge was completed in November 1980. In the 1990s, bridge plans were removed; by 2007, the replacement trench had replaced as the roadway’s predecessor.[14] By the 1970s, the bridge was adapted for the water-free route, eliminating congestion on thawed trains.[15]

Proposed work [ edit ]

Further reconstruction of the bridge would begin. In 2008, the exposed stones would be removed. In 2011, dredging wire had been installed and a steel beam would be removed.[16] In May 2015, a final masonry scaffolding had been installed and the replacement trench has been removed. The final work was completed by Mississauga in January 2016, about a year after the tunnel was opened.[17]
